This source document was not pre-segmented with sentence IDs, so evidence tags (E1, E2, ...) are paraphrase-anchored references to specific statements in the provided text rather than exact sentence indices.

components.description: Motivation: static-fairness dominance, statistical-fairness limitations in TTE, and the resulting research gap.

nodes.name: Fair ML largely static
nodes.description: Existing works in fair ML cover bias detection, fair prediction, and fair decision-making, but largely focus on static settings.

nodes.name: TTE fairness underexplored
nodes.description: Fairness in temporal contexts, particularly survival/time-to-event (TTE) analysis, remains relatively underexplored.

nodes.name: Existing TTE fairness uses statistical definitions
nodes.description: Current approaches to fair survival analysis adopt statistical fairness definitions rather than causal ones.

nodes.name: Statistical definitions can't disentangle causal mechanisms
nodes.description: Statistical fairness definitions, even with unlimited data, cannot disentangle the causal mechanisms that generate disparities.

nodes.name: Causal fairness literature mostly static
nodes.description: Causal fairness literature introduces important causal fairness notions but is concerned with the static setting only, with few dynamic-setting exceptions.

nodes.name: Gap: causal reasoning for TTE fairness
nodes.description: There remains a need for a deeper understanding of how causal reasoning can be applied to fairness in temporal/TTE data, which this paper aims to fill.

components.description: Standard Fairness Model (SFM) adapted to survival analysis, and the resulting two independence assumptions it encodes.

nodes.name: SFM adapted to survival setting
nodes.description: The Standard Fairness Model (SFM) cluster causal diagram is adapted to survival analysis, with protected attribute X, confounders Z, mediators W, survival time T, and censoring time C.

nodes.name: T, C unobserved; (M, δ) observed instead
nodes.description: T and C are assumed unobserved; instead the pair (M, δ) is observed, where M = min(T,C) and δ indicates whether the observed event is death.

nodes.name: No bidirected T–C edge implies conditional independence
nodes.description: Absence of a bidirected arrow between T and C in the SFM implies T ⊥ C | X, Z, W, i.e., the censoring mechanism is conditionally independent of the survival mechanism.

nodes.name: Conditional independence enables standard survival tools
nodes.description: The T ⊥ C | X,Z,W assumption allows application of standard survival-analysis tools such as conditional Kaplan-Meier and Nelson-Aalen estimators.

nodes.name: No further bidirected edges among {T,C,M,δ} and {X,Z,W}
nodes.description: The SFM further encodes lack-of-confounding assumptions: no bidirected edges between {T,C,M,δ} and {X,Z,W}, and none between X,W or Z,W.

nodes.name: Lack-of-confounding enables effect identification
nodes.description: These lack-of-confounding assumptions are important for identifying the different causal effects of X on the survival curve.

components.description: Two-step decomposition strategy for the TV disparity measure, motivated directly by the two SFM assumption groups.

nodes.name: TV disparity measure defined
nodes.description: The total variation measure TV_{x0,x1}(t) = P(T>t|X=x1) - P(T>t|X=x0) is used to quantify survival differences across demographic groups at time t.

nodes.name: Goal: decompose TV into pathway contributions
nodes.description: The goal is to decompose the TV disparity into contributions from the direct (X→T), indirect (X→W→T), and spurious (X⇢Z→T) pathways.

nodes.name: Two-step process mirrors the two SFM assumption groups
nodes.description: The decomposition proceeds in two steps closely related to the two types of assumptions encoded in the SFM: Step 1 (inference of P(T|X,Z,W)) and Step 2 (inference of causal effects of X on functionals of P(T|X,Z,W)).

nodes.name: Step 1: infer P(T|X,Z,W) via conditional independence
nodes.description: Under T⊥C|X,Z,W, the likelihood for T depends only on (M,δ), so conditional Kaplan-Meier/Nelson-Aalen estimators validly recover P(T|X,Z,W).

nodes.name: Step 2 setup: define Φ as a functional of P(T|X,Z,W)
nodes.description: Given P(T|X,Z,W), a mapping Φ = ϕ(P(T|X,Z,W)) is defined so the TV measure can be rewritten as E[Φ|X=x1] - E[Φ|X=x0].

components.description: The Causal Reduction Theorem (Thm 1) and the resulting decomposition/identification results.

nodes.name: Φ is a deterministic function of X,Z,W
nodes.description: Theorem 1 (Causal Reduction) shows that Φ's structural mechanism f_Φ(x,z,w)=ϕ(P(T|X=x,Z=z,W=w)) makes Φ a deterministic function of X,Z,W, not depending on noise variables.

nodes.name: Φ can be added to the causal diagram
nodes.description: Because Φ is a deterministic function of X,Z,W, it can be added as a new node to the causal diagram, yielding a reduced causal model.

nodes.name: Direct/indirect/spurious Φ-effects defined
nodes.description: Using the reduced model, x-specific direct (x-DE), indirect (x-IE), and spurious (x-SE) effects of X on Φ are defined analogously to standard causal fairness effects.

nodes.name: TV(Φ) decomposes into DE, IE, SE
nodes.description: The TV_{x0,x1}(Φ) disparity measure decomposes as TV = x-DE - x-IE - x-SE, following prior causal-fairness decomposition results.

nodes.name: Decomposition holds at each time point
nodes.description: Because Theorem 1 applies to Φ(t) for any t, the pathway decomposition of disparity can be performed at each individual time point, yielding a time-resolved explanation of disparity evolution.

nodes.name: Effects identifiable under the SFM (Prop. 1)
nodes.description: Proposition 1 shows that, under the SFM, the potential outcome E[Φ_{xy,W_xw}(t)|X=xz] is identifiable as a weighted sum over Z,W of conditional expectations of Φ, using estimable propensities.

components.description: Estimation strategies for the identified causal effects: model-based (RSF) and doubly-robust.

nodes.name: RSF used for model-based estimation
nodes.description: Random survival forests (RSF) are used to non-parametrically estimate P(T|X,Z,W) via the conditional cumulative hazard function, from which the survival function is obtained.

nodes.name: Model-based estimator of causal effects (Prop. 2)
nodes.description: Proposition 2 gives a plug-in model-based estimator for the potential outcome E[Φ_{xy,W_xw}(t)|X=xz] using the fitted f(x,z,w) and estimated propensities.

nodes.name: Time-invariant covariates make time-decomposition cheap
nodes.description: Because X,Z,W are time-invariant in this setting, the estimated propensities do not depend on time, making the temporal causal decomposition computationally inexpensive.

nodes.name: Doubly-robust estimator derived (Thm 2)
nodes.description: Theorem 2 derives a novel influence function for the potential outcome ψ under censored data, enabling doubly-robust debiasing of the model-based estimator.

nodes.name: Cross-fitting used for debiased estimation
nodes.description: The influence function is used with cross-fitting: nuisance functions are fit on one fold via xgboost while the influence function is evaluated on the remaining fold, with folds swapped to obtain a one-step debiased estimate.

components.description: Extension to competing risks: why joint event-time distributions are infeasible and CIFs are used instead.

nodes.name: Multiple event types motivate competing risks setting
nodes.description: Individuals may be simultaneously at risk of multiple distinct event types, motivating the competing risks (CR) extension beyond the basic non-informative-censoring case.

nodes.name: Only minimum event time observed
nodes.description: In the CR setting only M = min(T1,...,TK,C) and the event-type indicator δ are observed, not the individual event times.

nodes.name: Competing events may have unobserved common causes
nodes.description: Competing events may have unobserved common causes, represented as bidirected edges among T1,...,TK.

nodes.name: Full joint distribution generally infeasible to identify
nodes.description: Because only the minimum event time is observed and competing events may share unobserved causes, identifying the full joint distribution P(T1,...,TK|X,Z,W) is generally infeasible without strong assumptions like independence of failure times, which rarely hold.

nodes.name: CIFs used as the observable functional instead
nodes.description: As a result, most competing-risks approaches, including this work, focus on cumulative incidence functions (CIFs) rather than the full joint distribution.

nodes.name: CIFs account for competition between event types
nodes.description: CIFs explicitly account for competition: increasing one event type's rate necessarily reduces the CIFs of the remaining events, and CIFs sum with all-cause survival to 1.

nodes.name: Thm 1 applies to CIFs as Φ_k(t)
nodes.description: By the Causal Reduction Theorem, each Φ_k(t) := CIF_k(t) is a deterministic functional of P(T1,...,TK|X,Z,W) and hence a deterministic function of (X,Z,W), enabling the same direct/indirect/spurious decomposition for each cause k.

components.description: Extension to informative censoring via copula-based sensitivity analysis and the copula-graphic bounds theorem.

nodes.name: Informative censoring breaks T⊥C assumption
nodes.description: In the informative censoring (IC) setting, T ⊥ C | X,Z,W no longer holds (a bidirected T⇢C arrow exists), so standard survival-analysis tools are not directly applicable.

nodes.name: Inference requires additional assumptions
nodes.description: Because T⊥C|X,Z,W fails, inference of S(t|X,Z,W) is not possible without additional assumptions, motivating a sensitivity analysis approach.

nodes.name: Archimedean copula assumption adopted
nodes.description: The joint survival function H(t,c)=P(T>t,C>c) is assumed to follow an Archimedean copula parameterized by Kendall's τ, the sensitivity parameter.

nodes.name: Classical CGE assumes disjoint jumps
nodes.description: The classical copula-graphic estimator (CGE) assumes that at each grid point only one of S(t) or G(t) jumps, recursively identifying S(t) and G(t) from CIFs.

nodes.name: Fixed-grid CIF estimation violates disjoint-jump assumption
nodes.description: In this setting, estimation proceeds on a fixed grid of estimated CIFs where both Ŝ and Ĝ may jump at the same grid point, violating the classical CGE's disjoint-increment assumption.

nodes.name: Classical CGE must be adapted
nodes.description: Because the disjoint-jump assumption is violated, the classical CGE must be adapted: τ no longer uniquely identifies S(t_{i+1}), G(t_{i+1}).

nodes.name: Thm 3: sharp bounds under non-disjoint increments
nodes.description: Theorem 3 derives sharp, closed-form bounds on S(t_{i+1}) and G(t_{i+1}) given prior values and CIF increments, which collapse to point estimates as the grid is refined.

nodes.name: Midpoint interpolation yields point estimates
nodes.description: Point estimates of S(t) and G(t) are obtained via midpoint interpolation of the derived bounds, yielding a point-identified estimator as the grid becomes refined.

nodes.name: Recovered Ŝ(t) enables Thm 1 decomposition under IC
nodes.description: After recovering Ŝ(t), the Causal Reduction Theorem is invoked again to compute direct/indirect/spurious effects of X on S(t), quantifying causal fairness under informative censoring via sensitivity analysis on τ.

components.description: Case study setup: ICU race-differential analysis and its causal-structure justification.

nodes.name: ANZICS APD cohort constructed
nodes.description: The case study uses the ANZICS Adult Patient Database, covering 181 hospitals across Australia (Jan 2023-Jul 2024), yielding 249,958 patients, 10,436 (~4.2%) Indigenous.

nodes.name: Indigenous status modeled as X, no reverse causation with Z
nodes.description: Indigenous status and sociodemographic variables may share common causes but neither causes the other, motivating the X⇢Z spurious relationship as in prior literature.

nodes.name: Clinical variables modeled as mediators W
nodes.description: Clinical variables are temporally downstream of X and Z (e.g., indigenous status may influence illness severity via healthcare-access disparities), justifying their role as mediators W.

nodes.name: Censoring is administrative, justifying NIC for death analysis
nodes.description: The censoring mechanism is related to the data extraction process (an administrative reason), justifying the non-informative censoring assumption for the death-outcome analysis.

nodes.name: Death censoring is informative for readmission
nodes.description: Death censoring has unobserved common causes with readmission (latent illness severity, unmeasured frailty, care quality), so the readmission analysis falls under informative censoring.

nodes.name: Two potential unmeasured confounders acknowledged
nodes.description: The causal structure has two acknowledged limitations: genetic variation may confound X→W, and geographic remoteness may confound X, W, and T jointly.

components.description: Case study findings: death disparities (NIC) reveal masked opposing pathway effects.

nodes.name: TV measure near zero after T=80 days
nodes.description: The raw TV disparity measure for death rises then falls, with confidence intervals including 0 after T=80 days, appearing to suggest little disparity.

nodes.name: Direct effect favors minority patients
nodes.description: The direct effect decreases up to T=50 days then stabilizes, with its sign implying minority patients experience improved survival along the direct path.

nodes.name: Indirect effect harms minority patients, growing over time
nodes.description: The indirect effect decreases over time, implying reduced minority survival along this pathway (due to higher chronic/acute illness burden), reaching ~3% difference by T=50 days and continuing to amplify to T=180 days.

nodes.name: Spurious effect favors minority patients, growing over time
nodes.description: The spurious effect increases up to T=180 days, implying improved minority survival along the spurious pathway, related to lower average age at admission.

nodes.name: Decomposition reveals masked opposing effects
nodes.description: Together, the near-zero TV measure masks substantial, opposing pathway-specific effects — a pattern that would be missed by standard statistical fairness analysis.

edges.note: cross-component link from C4: time-resolved decomposition enables detecting the masked pattern

components.description: Case study findings: readmission disparities (IC) via sensitivity analysis.

nodes.name: TV measure for readmission increases over time
nodes.description: The readmission TV measure increases over time, indicating higher readmission burden for minority patients.

nodes.name: Route II sensitivity analysis applied with τ>0
nodes.description: Sensitivity analysis is performed via Route II (population-level copula) with τ ∈ {0.1,0.5,0.8}, assuming T1,T2 are positively correlated due to shared causes.

nodes.name: Direct/indirect effects show higher minority readmission burden
nodes.description: Along both the direct and indirect pathways, minority patients show increased readmission burden, with the indirect effect attributed to more complicated admission diagnoses and worse chronic health.

nodes.name: Spurious effect favors minority patients again
nodes.description: Along the spurious pathway, minority patients again show lower readmission burden, likely due to lower average age at ICU admission.

nodes.name: Confidence bounds limit definitive conclusions on direct effect
nodes.description: Despite the directional findings, the confidence bounds for the direct effect do not allow definitive conclusions about effect sizes.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: formalize causal fairness for TTE + Causal Reduction Theorem
nodes.description: Causal fairness is formalized for survival analysis, proving the Causal Reduction Theorem that enables identification and decomposition of group disparities in TTE settings.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: three regimes instantiated with identification results
nodes.description: The framework is instantiated in three regimes (non-informative censoring, competing risks, informative censoring), with identification results derived for each (Prop. 1).

nodes.name: Contribution 3: two new technical results (Thm 2, Thm 3)
nodes.description: Two new technical results are proven: a doubly robust estimator for censored data, and sharp bounds for copula-graphic estimation under non-disjoint increments.

nodes.name: Contribution 4: real-world ICU case study
nodes.description: Race differentials in post-ICU mortality are analyzed, demonstrating that causal fairness for TTE yields scientific insights missed by standard statistical fairness analyses.

isolated_nodes.name: Non-parametric focus distinguishes from prior mediation-survival work
isolated_nodes.description: Unlike most causal mediation literature for survival analysis, which adopts parametric models, this work focuses on non-parametric inference, avoiding strong distributional assumptions.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding in mediation
isolated_nodes.description: Developing sensitivity analyses for causal decompositions in the presence of unmeasured confounding (e.g., genetic variation, geographic remoteness) is left as an important future direction.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: relax copula family assumption
isolated_nodes.description: The choice of Archimedean copula family in the informative censoring setting is itself an additional modeling assumption that future work could relax.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: time-varying covariates and isolating competing-risk effects
isolated_nodes.description: The current formulation assumes time-invariant covariates and does not isolate primary from competing hazard effects in the competing-risks analysis; both are left for future extensions.
